title: Biological restoration of the osteoarthritic synovial joint

concept.text: The proposed innovation is to restore an established osteoarthritic human joint biologically: rebuild a continuous, load-bearing articular surface and recover useful, durable joint function. Its intended scope includes diffusely diseased joints and, ultimately, joints with widespread full-thickness cartilage loss. The supplied evidence describes regenerative goals and partial advances, but does not demonstrate this whole-joint capability in humans.

As a synthesis of the proposed capability, restoration would mean more than adding cartilage thickness. The target is organized hyaline articular tissue, rich in type II collagen, with appropriate depth-dependent organization, integration with underlying bone, and mechanical performance under repeated movement. A joint-level treatment would also need to address whichever surrounding conditions prevent lasting recovery, potentially including abnormal subchondral bone, synovial inflammation, meniscal dysfunction where relevant, and impaired lubrication. These are proposed engineering requirements; the supplied texts do not establish that every component must be separately regenerated in every patient.

significance.text: The GBD 2021 Osteoarthritis Collaborators estimated that 595 million people worldwide had osteoarthritis in 2020, with a 95% uncertainty interval of 535–656 million. Their 2023 report described the absence of an effective cure and identified joint replacement as highly effective for late-stage hip and knee disease, while noting affordability and access limitations. This establishes a large unmet need, although the global prevalence estimate is not an estimate of how many people would qualify for a particular regenerative treatment.

Conditional on achieving both lasting structural restoration and meaningful clinical recovery, this capability could allow eligible patients to retain a functioning biological joint and delay or avoid arthroplasty. That would be a major change in the treatment of advanced disease. Benefits for younger adults, extensively denuded joints, and patients outside the initially studied joint or disease stage would require direct demonstration. A regenerative treatment would also need a practical delivery and cost profile before improved access could be inferred.

The distinction between structural repair and patient benefit is central. In the FORWARD trial, a measurable increase in cartilage thickness did not produce a statistically significant total WOMAC advantage in the overall reported comparison. Accordingly, neither imaging thickening alone nor pain relief alone would establish the proposed combination of biological restoration and clinical recovery. Arthroplasty remains an effective treatment; the significance of regeneration would depend on demonstrated durability, safety, function, and avoidance of otherwise indicated surgery.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is durable restoration of a mechanically functional articular surface across a diffusely osteoarthritic human joint, accompanied by sustained clinical recovery. The supplied sources establish an unmet regenerative goal and limited structural progress, rather than an absolute biological impossibility of adult cartilage regeneration. They also do not establish that approval of a disease-modifying drug, if achieved, would by itself demonstrate reversal of established clinical disease.

As an engineering synthesis, the challenge includes producing sufficient cartilage matrix over a broad surface; organizing it into tissue with suitable zonal architecture and mechanics; integrating it with underlying bone and adjacent tissue; and maintaining it through years of cyclic loading. Structural repair must coexist with control of the diseased joint environment. These requirements preserve the original whole-joint reasoning without treating the supplied evidence as proof that matrix loss, bone pathology, inflammation, and integration failure form the same necessary causal combination in every case.

Restoring a denuded surface poses a further unresolved question: a treatment that stimulates surviving cartilage cells may not be sufficient where the relevant cells and matrix are largely absent. An engineered cell supply or living osteochondral construct could be an additional route, but the supplied evidence does not establish that either is necessary. Pharmacological regeneration, senescence-targeted interventions, local cell engineering, and constructs should therefore be assessed as possible routes to the same joint-level capability, with their sufficiency still to be demonstrated.

current_state.text: On 23 March 2026, Ken Garber reported in Nature Reviews Drug Discovery that developers had not secured FDA approval for a disease-modifying osteoarthritis drug and that Biosplice Therapeutics had recently submitted a new drug application for lorecivivint. The supplied review retains only the article's lead text; the body was paywalled. These are dated statements about U.S. regulatory development, not a comprehensive determination of worldwide approval status through 1 November 2026. Submission of an application does not establish approval or whole-joint restoration.

The 2019 JAMA FORWARD report provides a concrete example of structural improvement with uncertain clinical significance. At two years, sprifermin 100 μg administered every six months increased total femorotibial cartilage thickness by 0.05 mm versus placebo, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.03–0.07 mm. The corresponding every-twelve-month regimen produced a 0.04 mm difference. Neither regimen showed a statistically significant total WOMAC advantage in the reported overall comparison. The authors considered the clinical importance of the structural result uncertain. The supplied review assessed the abstract and ancillary bibliographic record, rather than the complete article; these findings do not establish restored tissue architecture, native mechanics, or reversal of advanced joint disease.

On 20 October 2026, Washington University described an ARPA-H-supported program intended to move a single-injection treatment for reversing joint damage toward clinical trials. Its institutional report described regeneration in animal models and stated that human trials were not expected to begin for at least another 18 months, with timelines subject to change. That timeline was a projection. The program was not evidence of completed human treatment, durable clinical benefit, or restoration of a denuded human joint.

An additional research assertion remains unverified within the supplied evidence: the earlier research attributes to Singla and colleagues a Science report on inhibiting 15-hydroxyprostaglandin dehydrogenase, with hyaline-cartilage regeneration in aged and injured mouse knees and human osteoarthritis explants, attributed to preexisting chondrocytes rather than stem cells. It supplies DOI 10.1126/science.adx6649, an alleged online date of 27 November 2025, and a conflicting March 2026 issue-date account. The validated review had neither the article text nor the second bibliographic record available, so the experiments, mechanism, and publication chronology cannot be confirmed here. If substantiated, animal and explant findings would still leave restoration of a denuded surface inside a living human joint unresolved.

The earlier research also reports October 2026 company statements about European application validation for lorecivivint, but those statements were not retained in the reviewed evidence. They cannot establish European regulatory status here. No FDA decision letter is included in the supplied materials; its absence does not establish whether a later decision occurred. More broadly, the supplied review contains no bounded freshness search establishing comprehensive coverage through 1 November 2026. The defensible conclusion is that these materials do not demonstrate durable whole-joint restoration in humans, while leaving later or unrepresented developments open.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: treat people with established symptomatic knee osteoarthritis, including a prespecified group with widespread full-thickness cartilage loss, and show restoration of a contiguous type II collagen articular surface with zonal organization and integration with underlying bone. Pair the structural outcome with clinically meaningful improvements in pain and function and durable avoidance of otherwise indicated arthroplasty. A single treatment or short course, followed by at least five years of ordinary activity, is a proposed ambition rather than a published consensus threshold.
completion_criteria.label: Restore contiguous articular surfaces and durable osteoarthritic knee function

completion_criteria.text: A convincing protocol should define baseline surgical eligibility, comparison care, validated pain and function outcomes, and how avoidance of arthroplasty will be attributed to clinical recovery rather than deferred access or changing patient preferences. Tissue assessment should establish the organization and integration of the repaired surface, with a justified relationship between imaging, any tissue sampling, and mechanical function. Loading exposure, retreatment, failures, and safety should be tracked alongside average benefit. These are proposed assessment requirements motivated by the distinction between measurable cartilage thickening and meaningful clinical recovery.
completion_criteria.label: Document attributable clinical recovery with integrated tissue and mechanical assessment

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: comparable results should be reproduced across independent clinical teams and defined patient groups, with advanced cartilage-loss cases reported separately. Studies should establish where the treatment works, where it fails, and whether delivery, rehabilitation, manufacturing where applicable, and follow-up are practicable. A mouse joint, human cartilage explant, or focal defect repair alone would not satisfy this human joint-level criterion. Successful finite trials would establish demonstrated breadth within the tested populations and conditions, not literal universality across all osteoarthritic joints.
completion_criteria.label: Reproduce clinical results across independent teams and establish practical boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster comparison, based on the supplied concept titles: ORT-01, Adult epimorphic regeneration of a functional limb, shares the ambition of organized adult tissue regeneration but requires coordinated restoration of an entire limb. ORT-02 concerns recovery of an existing diseased joint and does not require limb regrowth. ORT-05, Restoration of the intervertebral disc as a living load-bearing organ, shares the goal of durable biological restoration under repeated loading, but concerns a different anatomical structure and functional environment.

ORT-04, Regeneration of the load-bearing tendon–bone enthesis, overlaps with ORT-02 in the challenge of integrating mechanically different tissues. Its endpoint is a functional tendon attachment, whereas ORT-02 requires a restored articular surface and joint-level clinical recovery. ORT-08, Anatomically precise and reversible control of osteogenesis, could be relevant to managing bone formation during osteochondral repair, but control of osteogenesis alone would not establish cartilage restoration. ORT-10, Single-episode restoration of segmental long bone by vascularized, remodelable bone, addresses a large bone defect rather than an osteoarthritic articulating joint.

ORT-09, Regeneration of a functioning growth plate, shares an interest in organized cartilage but targets longitudinal growth rather than the durable articular surface of an adult joint. ORT-06, Force-bearing skeletal muscle after volumetric muscle loss, and ORT-07, Meaningful motor and sensory recovery across long peripheral-nerve gaps, address separate components of musculoskeletal function. Their restoration could matter to overall limb performance, but neither substitutes for the joint-restoration endpoint.

ORT-03, Eradication of mature biofilm in bone and on orthopedic implants without removing the reconstruction, targets infection control and preservation of a reconstruction. It remains distinct from regeneration of a degenerative joint. Successful joint regeneration might conditionally reduce some patients' need for implants, but it would not establish biofilm eradication in patients who already have infected implants.

Within ORT-02, pharmacological regeneration, senescence-targeted approaches, engineered cells, and living osteochondral constructs are possible routes to the same capability rather than automatically separate innovations. Focal cartilage repair and meniscal or labral substitution have narrower or adjacent anatomical goals. The earlier research cites long-term matrix-induced autologous chondrocyte implantation outcomes and a historical meniscal-allograft comparison, but the supplied review could not verify those details. Its reference to historical item 9 must not be equated with roster entry ORT-09, which concerns growth-plate regeneration.

unresolved_issues: The Singla article, experimental methods, proposed preexisting-chondrocyte mechanism, and conflicting publication dates cannot be verified from the reviewed materials.

The review recommendation to remove the unverified Singla and October regulatory details entirely was not adopted. They were retained as clearly qualified research assertions to preserve potentially useful information without treating it as established evidence.
Lorecivivint's reported October 2026 European application validation and any subsequent FDA action remain unverified; the March report establishes only its dated statements.
No comprehensive freshness search was supplied, so the record cannot establish exhaustive scientific or regulatory status through 1 November 2026.
The cited long-term focal-repair outcomes, meniscal-allograft history, and identity of historical item 9 remain unverified.
Whether severely denuded joints can recover through stimulation of remaining cells alone, or require added cells or constructs, remains unresolved.

The proposed clinical demonstration still requires operational definitions for tissue organization, integration, loading, safety, surgical eligibility, and attribution of durable arthroplasty avoidance.

brief.title: Restoring joints damaged by arthritis
possible: People with osteoarthritis, a disease that damages joints and limits movement, could regain lasting use of a badly damaged joint. Treatment would rebuild its cartilage, the smooth tissue covering the ends of bones, so it could bear weight through everyday activity.
The goal includes joints where cartilage has disappeared across broad areas. Patients could keep a functioning biological joint and delay or avoid joint replacement surgery.
why: Osteoarthritis affects an estimated 595 million people worldwide. Restoring damaged joints would give eligible patients a way to recover movement and reduce pain while retaining their own joint.

sources.showed: Their analysis estimated that osteoarthritis affects 595 million people worldwide.
sources.cited_for: The scale of the need for treatments that restore joint function.
sources.not_established: Population estimates do not establish how many people could benefit from a regenerative treatment.

sources.showed: Garber reported that Biosplice Therapeutics had applied for US approval of lorecivivint, a drug intended to slow joint damage.
sources.cited_for: Drug developers are pursuing treatments intended to change the course of osteoarthritis.
sources.not_established: An application for drug approval does not demonstrate restoration of a damaged joint.

sources.showed: In the FORWARD trial, sprifermin increased knee cartilage thickness compared with placebo. It produced no statistically significant overall advantage on WOMAC, a measure of pain and function.
sources.quote: Compared with placebo, there were no statistically significant differences in mean absolute change from baseline in total WOMAC scores
sources.cited_for: Cartilage thickening and meaningful recovery are separate outcomes.
sources.not_established: The trial did not establish a restored, mechanically functional joint surface or durable clinical recovery.

sources.who: Farshid Guilak, Christine T. N. Pham and the Washington University team
sources.showed: The team reported repairing osteoarthritis damage in animals without surgery. Its treatment delivers genetic instructions that make joint cells respond to disease signals by producing repair proteins.
sources.quote: The second phase of funding was contingent on the team meeting its phase 1 milestones, by demonstrating in animal models that their treatment could regenerate osteoarthritis damage without any surgical intervention.
sources.cited_for: An animal demonstration of joint repair using cells that respond to disease signals.
sources.not_established: The treatment has not demonstrated durable restoration or clinical benefit in humans.

shown: Hochberg and colleagues demonstrated increased cartilage thickness in human knees, without a statistically significant overall improvement in pain and function. Washington University researchers reported joint repair in animals; their treatment had yet to reach human trials.
missing: No human treatment has demonstrated a continuous, weight-bearing cartilage surface across a broadly diseased joint.
Repair has yet to combine lasting tissue integration with meaningful recovery in pain and function.
Durable recovery has yet to be demonstrated in people with widespread loss of the full cartilage layer.

milestones.label: A rebuilt knee surface with lasting recovery
milestones.explanation: A short treatment course would have to restore organized cartilage joined to bone, improve symptoms and avoid otherwise needed replacement for five years, including severe cases. This would establish lasting joint restoration.

milestones.label: Recovery tied to integrated, mechanically functional tissue
milestones.explanation: Comparative studies would have to link organized, integrated repair to mechanical function and clinical recovery, while tracking safety and failures. This would distinguish recovery from simply postponing surgery.

milestones.label: Independent results with clear practical limits
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce recovery in defined patient groups, report advanced cases separately and establish practical delivery. This would show where treatment works and where it fails.

uncertain: It remains unclear whether joints with little cartilage left can recover by stimulating surviving cells or will need added cells or tissue.
How best to measure repaired tissue organization, attachment to bone and performance under everyday loads remains unresolved.
The treatment must address enough of the surrounding joint disease to keep the repaired surface functioning.

page.title: Osteochondral regeneration in osteoarthritis
page.definition: A treatment regenerates the load-bearing surfaces of a person’s own osteoarthritic synovial joint. It restores the articular cartilage and the subchondral bone immediately beneath it so the joint can move and carry load with less pain. Existing osteochondral scaffolds such as Agili-C treat localized knee lesions. The regeneration goal extends to damage across the joint surface, including in severe osteoarthritis.

goal.need: Osteoarthritis affected an estimated 595 million people worldwide in 2020 and accounted for 21.7 million years lived with disability. Exercise and pain medication can ease symptoms while joint damage progresses. Replacement is effective for late-stage hip and knee disease, but some patients cannot afford surgery. Repairing the damaged tissue could help people keep using their own joint and delay replacement. The benefit depends on whether people can move more easily and with less pain, something a cartilage thickness measurement alone cannot establish.

completion.title: Both tissues reach Grade 0 in humans and ≥85% regain full joint function within three months.
completion.criterion: In Phase I human trials, demonstrate safety and restore articular cartilage and subchondral bone to Grade 0 (native tissue with no signs of osteoarthritis), including defects at or beyond the size that cannot heal completely without treatment. Pain must be <3/10 on a visual analogue scale, load capacity approximately that of the unaffected opposite joint, and joint function fully restored within three months in ≥85% of cases. The cartilage and bone treatments must work together and permit needle-based or non-invasive delivery in one procedure without surgical tissue harvest. NITRO targets all stages of osteoarthritis in all synovial joints.
completion.set_by: ARPA-H, NITRO BAA 75N99223R0003, sections 1.2.2 and 1.3, Tables 1–4; Proposers' Day slides 31–32.
completion.threshold_quote:
Meets/Exceeds All Prior Criteria in Human
Clinical Phase I Trials
completion.basis: NITRO carries regeneration, loading, pain and function criteria into human trials. This is a programme target rather than a marketing-authorisation standard. FDA's 2018 draft guidance explains why structural changes alone cannot establish patient benefit. ARPA-H's programme page states that NITRO human trials have not begun.

milestones.title: A treatment returns osteoarthritic cartilage and bone to Grade 0 in laboratory models.
milestones.criterion: In vitro, in small-animal models, or in both, restore articular cartilage and subchondral bone from all stages of osteoarthritis to Grade 0, the native state. For each tissue, demonstrate regeneration of defects at and beyond the critical size at which the defect cannot heal completely without treatment.
milestones.set_by: ARPA-H, NITRO BAA, section 1.2.2 and Tables 2 and 4.
milestones.threshold_quote: Regenerate all IA bone and cartilage, regardless of OA stage, to Grade 0

milestones.title: In large animals, regenerated joints sustain load and ≥85% regain full function within three months.
milestones.criterion: In a large-animal model of osteoarthritis, meet the Grade 0 cartilage and subchondral bone targets. Show sustained physiological loading of the regenerated tissues compared with the corresponding tissues in the same animal’s unaffected opposite joint. Post-treatment pain must be <3/10 on the programme’s visual analogue scale, and ≥85% must regain full joint function within three months.
milestones.set_by: ARPA-H, NITRO BAA, section 1.2.2 and Tables 2 and 4, and Proposers’ Day slides 31–32.

milestones.title: A joint-regeneration candidate demonstrates safety in Phase I human testing.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate the safety of a candidate cartilage or subchondral bone regenerative treatment in a Phase I human trial.
milestones.set_by: ARPA-H, NITRO BAA, section 1.2.2, TA1/TA2 Phase I clinical-trial goals.

milestones.title: Treatment increases femorotibial cartilage thickness versus placebo at two years in knee osteoarthritis.
milestones.criterion: In primary knee osteoarthritis, measure the change from baseline to two years in total femorotibial cartilage thickness by MRI. Test the linear dose relationship and the overall treatment effect, each at a two-sided significance level of 5%. Estimate the difference in change between each active regimen and placebo with a 95% confidence interval.
milestones.set_by: Merck KGaA, FORWARD Phase II protocol EMR700692_006, sections 8.3.1 and 8.5.2. This is a knee-specific structural endpoint independent of the NITRO trial requirements.

change from baseline in cartilage thickness in the total
femorotibial joint as evaluated by MRI at 2 years.

milestones.title: The sponsor completes all enabling studies and submits an investigational new drug application.
milestones.criterion: Complete all studies needed to support the investigational new drug application for the regenerative treatment and submit the application to the FDA.
milestones.set_by: ARPA-H, NITRO BAA, section 1.2.2 and Tables 2 and 4.
milestones.threshold_quote: Complete all IND-enabling studies (& submit IND application)

not_found: NITRO specifies no single grading instrument for Grade 0, operational measure of full function, or multiyear human durability threshold for injectable regeneration.
No published human result satisfying the combined NITRO regeneration, loading, pain and function targets was located.
No hip or hand study was found meeting the combined Grade 0 laboratory target or the large-animal loading, pain and function targets.
No regulator or professional society statement was found disputing the value or feasibility of osteochondral regeneration as a research goal.

definition = "A treatment regenerates the load-bearing surfaces of a person\u2019s own osteoarthritic synovial joint. It restores the articular cartilage and the subchondral bone immediately beneath it so the joint can move and carry load with less pain. Existing osteochondral scaffolds such as Agili-C treat localized knee lesions. The regeneration goal extends to damage across the joint surface, including in severe osteoarthritis.". Reason: The definition needs to distinguish regeneration within the existing joint from both focal osteochondral repair and implantation of a replacement joint.

goal.need = "Osteoarthritis affected an estimated 595 million people worldwide in 2020 and accounted for 21.7 million years lived with disability. Exercise and pain medication can ease symptoms while joint damage progresses. Replacement is effective for late-stage hip and knee disease, but some patients cannot afford surgery. Repairing the damaged tissue could help people keep using their own joint and delay replacement. The benefit depends on whether people can move more easily and with less pain, something a cartilage thickness measurement alone cannot establish.". Reason: The current text quantifies the burden but leaves out what preserving a joint would change for patients and why cartilage growth alone is insufficient.

add statement by Arthritis Society Canada and partners, 2026: "Repair joint damage through regenerative approaches". Reason: The Canadian arthritis action plan names regenerative repair specifically in its osteoarthritis research priorities.

edit completion: title = "Both tissues reach Grade 0 in humans and \u226585% regain full joint function within three months."; criterion = "In Phase I human trials, demonstrate safety and restore articular cartilage and subchondral bone to Grade 0 (native tissue with no signs of osteoarthritis), including defects at or beyond the size that cannot heal completely without treatment. Pain must be <3/10 on a visual analogue scale, load capacity approximately that of the unaffected opposite joint, and joint function fully restored within three months in \u226585% of cases. The cartilage and bone treatments must work together and permit needle-based or non-invasive delivery in one procedure without surgical tissue harvest. NITRO targets all stages of osteoarthritis in all synovial joints."; threshold_quote = "Meets/Exceeds All Prior Criteria in Human\nClinical Phase I Trials"; threshold_ref = 5. Reason: The title can be read as requiring 85% of normal function, while NITRO requires full function in at least 85% of cases and explicitly carries the targets into Phase I.
add case "Ankle". Reason: The cited cell-therapy study registered ankle osteoarthritis separately and used an ankle-specific functional outcome.

edit m1: criterion = "In vitro, in small-animal models, or in both, restore articular cartilage and subchondral bone from all stages of osteoarthritis to Grade 0, the native state. For each tissue, demonstrate regeneration of defects at and beyond the critical size at which the defect cannot heal completely without treatment."; set_by = "ARPA-H, NITRO BAA, section 1.2.2 and Tables 2 and 4."; threshold_quote = "Regenerate all IA bone and cartilage, regardless of OA stage, to Grade 0"; threshold_ref = 4; refs = [4, 8, 25]. Reason: The laboratory criterion mixes a mouse cartilage result into the test and omits the programme’s threshold quotation.

edit m2: title = "In large animals, regenerated joints sustain load and \u226585% regain full function within three months."; criterion = "In a large-animal model of osteoarthritis, meet the Grade 0 cartilage and subchondral bone targets. Show sustained physiological loading of the regenerated tissues compared with the corresponding tissues in the same animal\u2019s unaffected opposite joint. Post-treatment pain must be <3/10 on the programme\u2019s visual analogue scale, and \u226585% must regain full joint function within three months."; set_by = "ARPA-H, NITRO BAA, section 1.2.2 and Tables 2 and 4, and Proposers\u2019 Day slides 31\u201332."; threshold_quote = "Full function \u22643mo post-op with\n\u226585% success"; threshold_ref = 5; refs = [4, 5, 9]. Reason: The revision supplies the large-animal threshold and its within-animal loading comparator while removing the award announcement from the criterion.

add milestone after m2: "The sponsor completes all enabling studies and submits an investigational new drug application.". Reason: NITRO sets a distinct preclinical safety and application milestone between large-animal efficacy testing and the first human trial.

edit m3: criterion = "Demonstrate the safety of a candidate cartilage or subchondral bone regenerative treatment in a Phase I human trial."; threshold_quote = "Demonstrate safety in human trials"; threshold_ref = 4. Reason: The sprifermin dose groups and safety findings are trial results rather than conditions of NITRO’s human safety test.

edit m4: title = "Treatment increases femorotibial cartilage thickness versus placebo at two years in knee osteoarthritis."; criterion = "In primary knee osteoarthritis, measure the change from baseline to two years in total femorotibial cartilage thickness by MRI. Test the linear dose relationship and the overall treatment effect, each at a two-sided significance level of 5%. Estimate the difference in change between each active regimen and placebo with a 95% confidence interval."; set_by = "Merck KGaA, FORWARD Phase II protocol EMR700692_006, sections 8.3.1 and 8.5.2. This is a knee-specific structural endpoint independent of the NITRO trial requirements."; threshold_quote = "change from baseline in cartilage thickness in the total\nfemorotibial joint as evaluated by MRI at 2 years."; threshold_ref = 11. Reason: FORWARD specifies a knee MRI endpoint, and the existing criterion mixes its prespecified tests with the observed treatment effect.
remove not found 1. Reason: The existing search note treats the absence of a femorotibial MRI result in the hip or hand as an evidence gap even though the endpoint requires knee anatomy.

add not found: "No hip or hand study was found meeting the combined Grade 0 laboratory target or the large-animal loading, pain and function targets.". Reason: The hip and hand search finding still applies to the joint-independent laboratory and large-animal criteria.

add not found: "No regulator or professional society statement was found disputing the value or feasibility of osteochondral regeneration as a research goal.". Reason: Published doubts about individual treatments do not establish opposition to the regeneration goal itself.
remove statement 1. Reason: The cited NIAMS priority covers tissue restoration across skin and musculoskeletal diseases and does not name osteochondral regeneration in osteoarthritis as its goal.
